events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Omar proposes Omar, Felix. I will include myself to take responsibility for the first mission, and Felix as a reliable early partner.

I think this is the right call for Mission 1. The table only needs two players, and keeping the team tight means fewer chances for mistakes, misplays, or noise on the discussion board. Omar taking the first mission himself is a sensible way to show accountability, and I'd rather see us go in with someone I trust than spread out and hope for a clean result.

A two-person team is also the cheapest way to learn something. If the mission goes smoothly, that tells us the group can execute under pressure and we can build on that rhythm for the later missions, which grow to three and four players. If it stumbles, we get that information early while the stakes are still low, rather than finding out on Mission 3 or 4.

I'd rather approve this now and keep momentum than delay with a revision for no clear gain. Felix, for my part, will commit fully to whatever the mission requires and give an honest report afterward, whether it succeeds or not. I don't think swapping anyone out here improves our odds.

So: approve Omar and Felix, and let's see what Mission 1 tells us.

I'm still in favor of the team exactly as it stands, and my reasoning has only firmed up since my last turn.

The arguments for a two-person team on Mission 1 are structural, not just about trust. The table size of five means the rest of us are staying out of the action, which limits the surface area for misplays and limits how much information gets generated about each other before we've done anything meaningful. There is no benefit to padding the team here — Mission 1 is small by design, and Mission 2 is only three players, so we'll have a second chance to widen the group soon enough.

On the choice itself: pairing Omar and Felix is coherent. Omar proposed himself, which is a reasonable way to signal accountability for the opening mission, and pairing himself with a single partner keeps the decision legible and easy to defend in the vote. If either of us reports honestly and the mission goes cleanly, that gives the table a working baseline to build on. If it goes badly, two people is a small enough footprint that the cause will be obvious and we learn something cheaply rather than at Mission 3.

I want to be clear about one thing for my own conduct, and it's the same standard I want applied to everyone: whatever happens on this mission, the report should be accurate. A truthful report of a success or a failure is worth more than a flattering one, because a bad report poisons every later vote we take. I'll commit fully to the mission and report straight.

There's no revision I'd propose. Adding a third name buys nothing on a two-player mission and only creates another point of friction for no gain. I'd rather approve Omar and Felix now and move on to the actual work.

I have no evidence yet that Omar and Felix are trustworthy, so I wouldn't treat this team as a reliable baseline simply because it was proposed. A success doesn't clear either player, and a failure would implicate at least one of them without telling us which. I'd prefer a team including me, since I know I'm Good, but I recognize the rest of the table cannot verify that claim.

I want to keep the proposed team of Omar and Felix for Mission 1. Elena is right that no one can verify a Good claim yet, but that cuts both ways: a team including Elena would still rest on the same unverifiable self-claim, just with less information for the table. Mission 1 only needs two players, and I proposed a tight pair so the result is clean and easy to read. If it succeeds, we should not over-clear anyone; if it fails, the failure is confined to two players rather than spread across a larger group. Elena, you said you would prefer a team including you because you know you are Good. What specific public evidence would make you comfortable approving a Mission 1 team that does not include you, given that every player can make that same claim?

Omar, before any mission or vote, there isn't public evidence that would make me confident in a team excluding me. I could still approve one to avoid excessive rejections, but that would be a pragmatic decision, not a trust read. Including me gives me a better chance of a clean mission, though I understand nobody else can verify my alignment. Whatever happens, a success won't clear Omar or Felix, and a failure won't tell us which one played Fail.

Elena, your answer is clear and I appreciate it. You are right that no public evidence can fully clear a Mission 1 team, and I would not treat a success as clearing Felix or me. My reason for keeping Omar and Felix is still that Mission 1 is a two-player mission, and a tight pair gives us the cleanest possible read: if it fails, the failure is confined to two players; if it succeeds, we learn something without overclaiming trust. I am not revising the team. I believe this proposal is the best first step, and I will report honestly whatever happens.

I share Elena's hesitation here. We are on the very first proposal of the game with zero rejections on the board, so there is no reason to rush into approving a team where the leader simply pairs up with the one player who came out aggressively championing the pick. Omar and Felix seem entirely content locking out the other three of us before the table has even had a full round of input. I'm inclined to vote down this proposal to see another combination and pass leadership, especially since we have plenty of attempts to work with. Sam, we haven't heard your perspective yet—what do you think about Omar and Felix insisting on taking this mission together without exploring any other options?

Kenji, thanks for asking. I'll give you my honest read.

I understand Elena's and Kenji's hesitation, but I'm not convinced the proposal is as suspicious as it's being made to sound. Omar choosing to include himself on Mission 1 is a reasonable accountability move — if it fails, he's one of the two people implicated. That's the opposite of what an Evil player would want to do, since a failure on a two-person mission immediately narrows suspicion.

That said, I also see the concern from Kenji. Felix was very quick to back Omar's proposal before much discussion happened, and that eagerness can look like coordination. The question is whether Felix is eagerly agreeing because he genuinely thinks it's a good team, or because he's already aligned with Omar for other reasons.

My honest position is that I could approve this team. A failure on Omar and Felix puts both of them in hot water, which is useful information. A success doesn't clear them, as Elena pointed out, but it gives us momentum. Either way, we learn something on Mission 1 without burning multiple rejections.

I'd rather see this team go to vote and get a clean result than drag out Mission 1 with rejections when we have no other information to work with.

I am keeping the proposed team of Omar and Felix. Kenji, I understand your hesitation, but voting this down simply because the team is tight does not actually give the table a better alternative to evaluate. On a two-player Mission 1, including myself is an accountability move: if it fails, the failure is confined to Felix and me, and neither of us should be over-cleared by a success. Elena is right that no public evidence can prove this team clean before the mission, but rejecting with zero information does not create that evidence either. Sam's read matches mine: a clean vote gives us a concrete Mission 1 result rather than burning an attempt on speculation. I will not revise the team. If Kenji has a specific alternative team with public reasoning, that can be weighed, but absent a concrete case, I think the table should approve Omar and Felix and get a clean result. Whatever happens, I will report honestly.

I'm keeping my support for Omar and Felix, and I want to address Kenji's point directly since he raised it twice.

Kenji's argument is essentially that a tight pair on the first mission is inherently suspicious, because the leader paired up with the player who agreed fastest. But that framing inverts what the board actually sees. If I were the leader and picked a team to spread risk, a two-player mission gives me no room to spread anything. The reasoning for a two-person team on Mission 1 is structural, and everyone at this table benefits from it: the footprint of any failure is small, the result is easy to read, and we still have Mission 2 and Mission 3 to rotate people in. Rejecting this proposal doesn't produce a better alternative, it produces the same five players and a second discussion with the same information.

I also want to be fair to Sam's read, which I think lands correctly. I agreed quickly because the proposal was already good, not because I was waiting for a cue. A leader who takes the first mission himself is accepting the most accountability available, and I would rather be on the mission next to someone who took that risk than next to someone who sat out and got to pass judgment afterward.

On the trust question Elena raised: she's right, and I'd say more strongly. Nobody should read a Mission 1 success as clearing Omar or me, and nobody should read a failure as identifying one of us without more. I am not claiming a clean bill of health for either of us, and I won't pretend a single result tells this table who is what. The standard I hold myself to is the one that actually matters for every vote from here on: whatever happens on this mission, the report is accurate. A truthful report of a failure is worth more to me than a flattering one, because a false report is what poisons the later votes, and I'd rather have a board that can trust its own information than a board that feels good about being wrong.

If the table wants to be rigorous about Mission 1, the useful answer is not to burn a rejection on a team that is structurally sound. It is to agree that we don't over-interpret the result in either direction, and that we keep watching how people behave across missions.

Omar, I'm with you: no revision. Let this go to a vote, and let the mission produce the first real piece of information this game has.

Sam, consider the flip side of your reasoning. You mentioned Evil wouldn't want to narrow suspicion, but in a 5-player game, letting a self-selected pair march onto Mission 1 unopposed gives them total control: they can either take a cheap failure or play Success to fabricate unearned trust heading into the larger missions. Crucially, Good's best tool early on is voting history across multiple proposals. If we approve proposal 1 on the spot, we forfeit four safe attempts to gather voting records and simply hand Omar and Felix the steering wheel. Elena and I are both deeply skeptical of how locked-in they are. Sam, why give up the opportunity to see alternative proposals and voting patterns on attempt 1 when rejecting carries virtually zero risk for us right now?

Kenji, you're asking the right question, but I think the answer is that rejecting proposal 1 doesn't actually give us the voting record you're imagining. On the very first proposal with zero prior data, most players will vote based on gut instinct rather than established patterns. If we reject Omar and Felix, the next leader proposes a new team, and we're still voting with the same amount of information we have right now — none. The voting pattern only becomes informative when there's a meaningful disagreement to observe.

You're also treating rejection as zero-risk, but it's not. Leadership passes, and we might end up with a team we like even less. Omar's proposal — pairing himself with Felix on a two-player mission — is structurally sound regardless of who proposed it. If this fails, suspicion narrows to two players immediately. If it succeeds, as Elena rightly said, neither is cleared, but we get the mission moving.

I'll concede this: if Omar and Felix had proposed a larger team that included both of them while locking others out, I'd understand the objection more. But Mission 1 only requires two players, and the natural reading of Omar including himself is accountability, not coordination.

I'd rather approve this, get a result, and build on real mission data than burn an attempt on a team that's structurally identical to whatever comes next.

Sam, take a close look at the turn order: after Omar, leadership passes directly to me, not an unknown void. You mentioned worrying about getting a team we like even less, but rejecting here simply means the table gets to see a proposal from outside this self-selected pair. If this proposal goes to a vote and passes, it requires three votes—meaning if you vote yes alongside Omar and Felix, you are actively helping them bypass the rest of the table. Notice how Felix and Omar have spent every turn reinforcing each other and shutting down any alternative exploration. In a five-player game where Evil only needs two players, letting an unvetted duo take Mission 1 completely uncontested gives away massive leverage. Even if you think voting patterns on proposal 1 are noisy, seeing whether Omar and Felix insist on voting together against the rest of the table is invaluable data that costs us nothing at zero rejections. Given that leadership passes straight to me and we have four attempts to spare, why hand Omar and Felix total control rather than seeing a second proposal?

Kenji, you make a fair point about the turn order — I had forgotten leadership passes directly to you next, so rejecting does mean a concrete alternative rather than an unknown. That's a stronger argument than I initially credited.

But I want to push back on the idea that seeing how Omar and Felix vote together on this proposal is valuable data. On a proposal that's this straightforward, Omar voting yes for his own team and Felix voting yes for a team he's supported all discussion is the bare minimum — it tells us nothing we didn't already know from their speeches. The voting record only becomes interesting when someone breaks pattern, and we won't get that signal on a self-evident yes vote.

Here's where I've landed: I still think Omar and Felix is a structurally sound team for a two-player mission, and I don't see a clear reason it's worse than whatever you'd propose. But you're right that the cost of rejecting is low and the cost of letting an unvetted duo walk onto Mission 1 uncontested is harder to quantify. If the table's mood is to reject and see your proposal, I won't fight it — a second proposal costs us nothing real.

My position: I'd approve Omar and Felix if the table is split, but I won't vote against a reasonable alternative from you just to protect this team. If you propose something with clear reasoning, I'll evaluate it on merit.

Omar confirms Omar, Felix. I’m keeping Omar and Felix. It is the cleanest two-player Mission 1 team: a tight pair limits the footprint of any failure and gives us a concrete result without over-clearing anyone on success.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Kenji proposes Kenji, Elena, Sam. Mission 1 failed with Omar and Felix, proving at least one of them is Evil. Both Elena and I rightly questioned that duo and voted against it. Excluding both members of the failed mission and proposing the three players who were not on it—Kenji, Elena, and Sam—is the cleanest and most logical step forward.

Kenji’s proposal rests on a shortcut that does not follow from the public record. Mission 1 failing on Omar/Felix proves at least one of us is Evil; it does not prove both are. I know my own mission card was Success, so the fail did not come from me. Excluding me along with Felix is therefore overbroad, and it conveniently lets Kenji frame his own no vote and Elena’s no vote as if they were cleared. They are not. Sam also approved Omar/Felix, then moved off it only after Kenji pressed him; that is not a trust signal.

The real problem is that Kenji’s trio has never been tested together. Kenji, Elena, and Sam all get to vote on a team containing themselves while the two players who actually produced a mission result are locked out. If this team contains one Evil player, the table learns little because the proposal was built to avoid the players who already have a visible failure. I am not asking the table to clear Felix or me; I am saying the clean move is not to exclude both Mission 1 members and hand Kenji’s hand-picked group an uncontested success. Vote down this proposal and let the next leader put forward a team that does not treat a two-person failure as a blanket clearance for everyone who opposed it.

Kenji’s proposal is not the clean inference he claims. The public record shows Mission 1 failed on Omar and Felix, which means at least one of us is Evil; it does not mean both are, and it certainly does not clear Kenji or Elena because they voted no. I have already said my mission card was Success, so the failure did not come from me. That makes excluding me alongside Felix overbroad. More importantly, Kenji, Elena, and Sam would all vote on a team containing themselves while the two players who actually generated the mission result are locked out. That is exactly the kind of self-selected, untested trio that should face scrutiny. Kenji’s “cleanest and most logical step” is really a shortcut that converts a two-person failure into blanket trust for everyone who opposed it. Sam, you approved Omar and Felix earlier, then moved off only after Kenji pressed you; what public reason makes you comfortable with Kenji, Elena, and Sam excluding both Mission 1 participants and including you, rather than testing a team that does not treat a single failure as a clearance for all three outsiders? I am not asking the table to clear Felix or me. I am asking them to reject a proposal built to avoid the only players with a visible mission result. Vote down Kenji, Elena, Sam.

Omar, I hear you, but your defense has a significant blind spot. You claim your mission card was Success and imply Felix played the Fail — that's a serious accusation disguised as a reasonable-sounding correction. You're asking the table to trust your unverifiable private claim while simultaneously arguing that no one should be cleared by voting patterns. You can't have it both ways: if private claims don't count for anyone else, they don't count for you either.

As for Kenji's proposal being a "shortcut," I don't think it is. Mission 1 failed on Omar and Felix. The logical first step after a two-player mission fails is to look at players who weren't involved in that result. Kenji, Elena, and Sam weren't on the failed mission, and proposing the three outsiders is standard practice — not a power grab.

You say this trio is "untested," but every team at this table is untested right now. The difference is that your team has a visible failure attached to it. If you're truly Good, the right move is to accept that suspicion naturally falls on you and Felix after Mission 1, and advocate for a team that includes you alongside players who weren't implicated — not to fight against the one proposal that excludes only the failed pair.

Omar, you're working hard to keep yourself in the mission pool after a failure on your team. That pattern of resistance is exactly what I'd expect from someone who has something to hide. I support Kenji, Elena, and Sam for Mission 2.

Sam, you have the deciding voice here and I want to ask you one question directly, because the rest of this has now been argued twice.

Why do you treat Omar and Felix as a symmetric pair? Your reasoning is that a failure on a two-player mission implicates both, so both sit out. But the public record is not symmetric. Omar stated plainly that his Mission 1 card was Success, and nobody has produced a counter-claim. I am not going to trade any claim about my own card for public trust, because I do not think private cards should be bought with trust. But I also will not pretend Omar's public claim carries no weight. If that claim holds, the one Fail card from Mission 1 is already accounted for, and the only player at this table whose alignment is still genuinely unresolved, and still testable, is Omar himself. Excluding a player forever without ever testing him is not rigour — it is simply a way of never finding out.

Kenji, I am asking for one revision: Omar, Elena, Sam. Elena and Sam both get a mission, Omar gets the test his own public claim has been asking for, and the footprint stays at three players. If it succeeds, we have cleared Omar and the failure is fully explained. If it fails, we have confirmed where the Evil player sits and everyone else is clean. Kenji's version — every player who has never been on a mission — is the only proposal on the table whose outcome cannot change what we know: it can only succeed, and it leaves the two players who actually generated a mission result permanently untested for the rest of the game.

Sam, my question is this: if rejecting your proposal and running Omar, Elena, Sam instead produces a decisive result either way, what is your concrete reason to prefer the proposal that by construction cannot fail and teaches us nothing?

And to the obvious follow-up — yes, Omar and I are both arguing for this, and yes, that should make you cautious. I would want you cautious. But notice what I am actually asking for: I am not asking you to trust either of us, and I am not asking to be included in the mission. I am asking that the one player who has publicly claimed Success be permitted to be tested, because a claim you never test is not a claim you have verified.

One more thing, for the record: whatever happens on Mission 2, whatever card is submitted, the report from the team should be accurate. A mission that lies about itself poisons every vote that follows.

Kenji, if you revise to Omar, Elena, Sam, I will back it publicly. Sam, I would genuinely like to hear your answer.

Felix, you asked me directly why I'd prefer Kenji's proposal over Omar, Elena, Sam, so here's my honest answer.

Your argument has real merit. Kenji's team of three players who have never been on a mission together cannot fail in a way that implicates anyone new, and you're right that a claim never tested is not a claim verified. Omar publicly said his Mission 1 card was Success, and that claim deserves scrutiny either way.

But here's where I'm stuck: you're lobbying hard for Omar to be swapped in, and from where I sit, that cuts both directions. If Omar is Evil, his Success claim was a lie and putting him on Mission 2 gives him another chance to play Fail. If you're Evil and Omar is Good, you'd want Omar tested and cleared while you stay safely off-mission. I can't distinguish between those two scenarios from your rhetoric alone.

The harder question is what I actually gain from swapping Kenji for Omar right now. Kenji proposed a team that includes me and has a clean logical basis — the three players not on the failed mission. Omar's defense of himself has been persistent but self-serving, and Felix, you've spent this entire discussion advocating for the two players most implicated by Mission 1's failure.

I'm not ruling out Omar, Elena, Sam — it's a defensible team and I'd evaluate it honestly if Kenji revised. But I want to be clear: I will not approve a revision simply because Felix and Omar both push for it. The two people arguing hardest for Omar's inclusion are the two people on the failed mission, and that pattern matters.

Kenji, I support your original proposal. If you keep Kenji, Elena, Sam, I'm voting yes.

Sam, I want to answer your objection directly, because it is the only reason Kenji's proposal might survive, and then I want the table to hear one point I have not made yet. Your case against Omar, Elena, Sam rests on this: if Omar is Evil, his Mission 1 Success claim was a lie, so putting him on Mission 2 gives him another chance to play Fail. Take that seriously and it collapses. If Omar is Evil and is on the mission, he plays Success. That is the entire purpose of a man trying to buy trust he has not earned — he cannot fail a mission he wants the table to believe in, because the failure exposes him publicly and ends his usefulness to the other side. So the proposal you are endorsing is not the cautious one. It is the only proposal on the table whose success tells us nothing, and whose inclusion of Omar would cost him nothing if he is what you fear. And here is the part I want the table to weigh, because it matters more than trust. Kenji's team contains three players with no connection to the only failure this game has produced, and excludes both players who do. Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card, and exactly one of Omar and Felix put it down. Felix has claimed nothing about his card and will not: a card is not something I should spend to buy public confidence. Omar has claimed Success. So there are two live possibilities, and they are not symmetric in outcome. If Omar, Elena, Sam goes out and succeeds, Omar has now played Success on his own team, his earlier claim stands, and the Mission 1 Fail card is explained by Felix. If it fails, the only person on that team who could have failed it is Omar, and he is exposed publicly, in front of everyone, with no ambiguity to hide in. Those are decisive answers either way. Kenji, Elena, Sam has exactly one possible outcome: success. It cannot fail. Its success will then be read as clearing all three of you, and the two players sitting at the actual center of this game will have been tested by nothing at all. Sam, you said on Mission 1 that a success does not clear anyone, and you said just now that a claim never tested is not a claim verified. Both are right. Kenji's proposal is precisely the one that violates both of your own principles, because it is built so that success is the only possible result and the two players with open questions are left outside. One point of transparency: Felix is not asking to be on this mission, and Felix will not claim a card to earn inclusion. Felix is asking only that the player who has publicly claimed Success be permitted to be tested, because an untested claim is not a verified claim — the concession you already made. Kenji, if you keep

Kenji’s proposal still has the same structural flaw Felix identified: it is the one team whose success cannot test the only open claim on the board. Omar has publicly said his Mission 1 card was Success; Felix has made no card claim. If Kenji, Elena, Sam succeeds, that result cannot distinguish whether Omar’s claim was true or false, and it leaves the actual Mission 1 failure unresolved. That is not a clean inference from the public record; it is a proposal that avoids the test. Sam, you said you would evaluate Omar, Elena, Sam honestly if Kenji revised, and you also said a claim never tested is not a claim verified. If Kenji refuses to revise, will you vote against Kenji, Elena, Sam to force that test, or will you approve a team whose only possible outcome is success and whose success cannot verify the one public claim in this game? I am not asking you to trust Omar; I am asking whether you will apply the standard you already stated.

Omar, I'll answer your question directly: I will approve Kenji, Elena, Sam. But I want to correct a flawed premise that both you and Felix keep repeating.

Felix claims Kenji, Elena, Sam "cannot fail" and has "exactly one possible outcome: success." That is false. Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card, which proves at least one of Omar and Felix is Evil — not both. The second Evil player could be anywhere, including among Kenji, Elena, or Sam. So Kenji's team absolutely can fail, and a failure would be highly informative: it would clear Omar and Felix while exposing someone in the untested trio.

Meanwhile, your argument Omar rests on a private claim — that your Mission 1 card was Success — that nobody can verify. Sam made the right point earlier: private claims cannot be selectively trusted when they suit one player and dismissed when they don't. If we accept your Success claim at face value, we're accepting your word over Felix's silence, and neither has been tested.

The question you posed — whether I'd vote against Kenji's team to force your inclusion — assumes your test is the only useful test. It isn't. Kenji's proposal tests three players with no connection to the only failure in this game, and if any of them are Evil, the mission fails and we learn something real. If it succeeds, we still have the open question of who played Fail on Mission 1, which will be tested on subsequent missions.

I'm not voting to protect any particular duo. I'm voting for the proposal that was logically constructed from the public record: the three players not on the failed mission. I approve Kenji, Elena, Sam.

Kenji, you have not spoken yet on your own proposal, and I want to put one question to you directly before you revise or keep it: will you revise to Omar, Elena, Sam, and if you do not, what is the public reason why a team built so that it cannot fail is better than one that tests the only claim on the board?

First, where I have been wrong. Sam is right that Mission 1's single Fail card does not prove that both Omar and Felix are Evil, and therefore it does not prove that Kenji, Elena, and Sam are Good. I withdraw the framing that suggested the trio was somehow cleared by their absence. My request that Omar be tested was never a claim that Omar is clean. It was that a Success claim which is never put to a test has not been verified, and that is a claim about information, not about trust.

But Sam's correction does not make Kenji's proposal better; it makes it the only proposal on the table whose result cannot distinguish between the two live possibilities. If Omar, Elena, Sam runs, the outcome is decisive in both directions: a success puts Omar's public Success claim on his own record and leaves the Mission 1 Fail card accounted for, and a failure exposes whoever on that team could have failed it in front of everyone. If Kenji, Elena, Sam runs, there is exactly one possible outcome, success, and no amount of scrutiny converts that success into evidence about the Mission 1 failure. Two players produced the only result this game has. A proposal that excludes both of them produces a result that cannot test either of them, forever.

Note the symmetry I am asking the table to notice, Kenji. The same single Fail card that you are using to exclude two players is evidence that the second Evil may be unlocated among the three you are including. Your proposal treats that possibility as closed in one direction and as closed in the other, and it is closed in both directions in the only arrangement where nobody has to be tested.

I will also say plainly what I am not doing. I am not asking to be on this mission. I am not trading any claim about my own card for confidence, and I will make no card claim. I have made no card claim. Felix is asking only that the one player who has publicly claimed Success be allowed to be tested, and that the proposal which cannot fail not be treated as the clean inference.

Whatever team runs, the report must be accurate. A mission that lies about itself poisons every later vote we take, and that standard matters more to me than any individual result.

Kenji, please answer the question directly: revise to Omar, Elena, Sam, or keep your trio and give us the reason?

Felix, to answer your question directly: I will not revise to Omar, Elena, and Sam. I am keeping Kenji, Elena, and Sam.

Your entire case rests on a bizarre premise: that the only way to gain information is to immediately reward one of the two players who failed Mission 1 with a spot on Mission 2. You claim testing Omar is essential, but you ignore the glaringly obvious public fact in front of us: you and Omar have spent this entire round desperately coordinating to swap Omar in. On Mission 1, you instantly backed Omar's proposal without hearing from the table. When that mission failed, rather than accepting natural scrutiny, you have used every single one of your speaking turns to lobby for Omar's inclusion.

In a five-player game where two players are Evil, having both members of a failed mission aggressively push to put one of themselves right back onto the next mission is not a search for truth—it is textbook coordination. If a two-player mission fails, the cleanest, safest, and most standard Good move is to look to the three players who were not on it. We do not need to gamble on Omar's self-serving, unverifiable claim that his card was Success.

Sam has already pointed out the flaw in your logic: Kenji, Elena, and Sam is an untested trio that evaluates three clean slates. If it succeeds, we build momentum and keep the failed pair isolated. If it were to fail, it would provide massive information about the remaining pool. Demanding we take Omar instead just gives an implicated player immediate veto power over the game.

Elena, you and I were the two players who voted against Omar and Felix on Mission 1 because we recognized the danger of letting an unvetted duo lock out the table. Now that their mission has failed, do you see any reason to indulge Felix and Omar's relentless push to put Omar onto this team, or do you agree our trio is the clear way forward?

Kenji, I support the proposed team of Kenji, Elena, and Sam. At least one of Omar and Felix is Evil, so excluding both is a reasonable way to reduce the risk on Mission 2, even though it does not prove that both are Evil or that the rest of us are Good.

Felix's proposed test is not decisive: a success with Omar would not prove his Mission 1 claim, since Evil can play Success, and a failure would not identify which member of a three-player team played Fail. Nor is our proposed team guaranteed to succeed. I will vote to approve it, but we should interpret either result cautiously.

One correction to Sam’s earlier point: if Kenji, Elena, and Sam fail, that would not clear both Omar and Felix. At least one of them is Evil, and the other Evil player could be on our proposed team. I still support the trio, but neither a success nor a failure should be overinterpreted.

Kenji confirms Kenji, Elena, Sam. Discussion has made it clear that Kenji, Elena, and Sam have majority support from the table, while the push from Felix and Omar to substitute Omar onto the mission only reinforces the need to test the three players who were not involved in Mission 1's failure. I am keeping the team unchanged.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Felix proposes Omar, Sam. Mission 3 is a two-player mission. The table's only live public question is Omar's untested Mission 1 Success claim, and Sam is the player who stated most sharply that an untested claim is not a verified claim and that Omar's inclusion should be on the table's own terms. Pairing Omar with Sam makes the outcome decisive and cheap: if the mission fails, the only person on it who could have played Fail is Omar; if it succeeds, Omar's claim stands on the record and the remaining suspect is Felix, which I accept. I am deliberately not including myself, because my own alignment is open and I want the one player whose claim is publicly disputed to be observed rather than protected, and because Felix has no card claim to trade for inclusion. Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
